name: Saraiki
confidence_why: Shackle's 1976 reference grammar (relayed by Bashir and Conners 2019) and Atta's 2021 phonology article, the only two independent first-hand descriptions, both give Saraiki a single quantity-sensitive main stress that falls on the initial syllable unless the second syllable is heavy (long vowel) and the first light, and they differ only on secondary stress, a handful of lexical exceptions and the phonetic cue.

new_statements.quote: All words, other than a very restricted set of enclitics (1.11.2), have one accented syllable. Words of more than two syllables may also have a secondary accent. [...] a) all words have first-syllable accent, except b) disyllables with weak pre-tonic and peripheral vowel + consonant or diphthong in the second syllable, like /saval/ 'question', /dtrkhan/ 'carpenter', /sazai/ 'punishments', which have final accent, and c) trisyllables with weak pre-tonic and peripheral vowel or centralized vowel + geminate in the second syllable, like Wicara/ 'poor', /evhattar/ 'seventy-four', which have second-syllable accent. The accent is noted in transcription only in unpredictable cases

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists Saraiki with an empty rule and no existing statements; Shackle supplies a full rule: initial by default, weight-driven shift to a heavy second syllable after a weak initial, residual lexical minimal pairs. Shackle's object is 'Siraiki' of central Pakistan (Multan-centred central dialect).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default first-syllable accent. If the first syllable is weak (centralized vowel, at most one following consonant) and the second syllable is heavy (peripheral vowel + consonant or diphthong in disyllables; peripheral vowel, or centralized vowel + geminate, in trisyllables), the accent moves to that second syllable (final in disyllables, second in trisyllables). Tonic syllable is marked chiefly by length (long peripheral vowel or gemination after a centralized vowel), realized against a post-tonic 'tail'. Transcription symbols in the quote are scanned-garbled (/dtrkhan/ = /ḍirkhān/ 'carpenter', Wicara/ = /vicārā/ 'poor', /evhattar/ = /cuhattar/ 'seventy-four').
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 28: 'Trisyllables in which the accent is on the first syllable have secondary accent on the third, i.e., allowing the interval of a syllable for the tail of the tonic to be realized, thus /"abar'gut/ 'suddenly'.' Words of more than three syllables occur only as compounds (§1.11.4); in compounds 'primary accent falls on the first member only' (§1.11.2 area, djvu line 2124).
new_statements.exceptions: pp. 28–29: accent is unpredictable (and noted) in (d) disyllables with weak pre-tonic and centralized vowel + consonant in the second syllable: /so'nhap/ 'beauty' vs. /'taraph/ 'agitation', /gha'sun/ 'punch' vs. /'ghusan/ 'to err'; and (e) disyllables with weak pre-tonic and final peripheral vowel: /bhi'ra/ 'brother' vs. /'bhari/ 'filled', /it'la/ 'informing' vs. /'itla/ 'so much' — 'The only minimal pairs differentiated by the position of accent belong to this class.' Enclitics are unaccented (§1.11.2); metathesis of initial clusters in derived forms postpones the accent, /'dhrokan/ but /dhor'kavan/ (p. 24 area, djvu line 1706).
new_statements.identity_note: Shackle 1976 describes 'Siraiki' of central Pakistan (the central, Multan-area dialect) and calls it Siraiki throughout. Bashir & Conners 2019 (TOC only) treat Saraiki alongside Hindko and Panjabi, with separate subsections 'Tone in Saraiki' (p. 49) and 'Stress in Saraiki' (p. 52), suggesting the book also addresses whether Saraiki shares the Panjabi tone system; that text was not accessible. Atta et al. 2020 is a JIPA Illustration titled simply 'Saraiki'.

readall_conflicts: The single listed work (Bashir & Conners 2019) could not be read beyond its table of contents, so it neither agrees nor disagrees with anything. Between the two sources already held by the project there is no conflict on placement: Shackle 1976 gives default initial accent with a weight-driven shift to a heavy second syllable after a weak initial, plus a residual class of lexical minimal pairs; Atta, van de Weijer & Zhu 2020 state no rule but their examples (initial in disyllables, second syllable in trisyllables with a heavy second syllable) fit Shackle's rules. They differ on the phonetic cue: Shackle says the tonic syllable is distinguished principally by length (vowel lengthening or gemination), Atta et al. say pitch rise and intensity, not necessarily duration. One minor tension: Atta et al.'s suː.ˈɦɑ̃ʤ.ɽɑ̃ 'moringa tree' has a long first syllable yet second-syllable stress, which Shackle's rule (c) (weak pre-tonic required) would not predict.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: every fragment of the deciding quotation and the the secondary-stress rule quotes are verbatim in the Atta 2021 text we hold at the stated pages (134-135, 137, 144) and in the held Bashir & Conners excerpt (pp. 52-53). Deciding source is a 2021 peer-reviewed phonology article devoted to Saraiki word stress, backed in the record by the 2019 Mouton reference grammar; that is the best available description. Two sources not previously held were downloaded: Shackle 1976 (sec. 1.10, pp. 27-29) independently confirms a quantity/vowel-peripherality-sensitive system with default initial accent, final accent when a weak (centralized-vowel) pretonic precedes a peripheral vowel + C, penult accent in the corresponding trisyllables, length as the main correlate, and a small lexically contrastive residue (bhi'ra vs 'bhari) — exactly the hedges that make 'weight-hedged / weight-sensitive (tentative)' the right class rather than strict
